newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rough times seen for Thai economy, stocks.
newsitem.headline: Rough times seen for Thai economy, stocks.

text.p: Schroder Investment Management Ltd said on Thursday that Thailand's battered economy and stock market would face more rough times this year, but should offer good investment opportunities in the next few years.
Schroder analysts said they were confident the Bank of Thailand would succeed in defending the baht against further pressure from currency speculators.

"We see possible short-term volatility and a risk that measures taken by the government may not be enough to stabilise property and financial sectors. But there are investment opportunities on a two-three-year view," said Douglas Cairns, Schroder's chief investment officer in Thailand.

Matthew Dobbs, Schroder Investment's regional managing director, told a seminar he would advise investors to start putting money in Thai equities from the second half of 1997, saying Thailand still belonged to a club of high growth Asian nations.
"We are currently pretty preoccupied with problems, but look at the near single-digit price/earnings ratio and company strength seen from some of our Thai company visits," he said.

Thai financial and property sectors have been shaken by growing non-performing loans arising from a four-year property slump. The Thai baht faced sporadic speculative attacks in December and February on concerns over weak exports and a high current account deficit.
Giles Neville, manager of Schroder's global emerging market fund, said his fund was currently underweight on Thailand but he expected it to switch to overweight soon.

"Thailand is not one that we have invested much lately, but historically we would invest more...we have seen the government taking steps to stabilise the system...when confidence returns, we could have equally sharp recovery being reflected in the stock market," he said.
Cairns said the investment return on Thai stocks was a 16 percent loss so far this year after a 35 percent decline in 1996.

The Thai SET Index underperformed most Asian countries, registering an 1.8 percent negative annualised investment return during 1993-1996 against average 17.7 percent growth for the Asia-Pacific region.

Schroder analysts praised Thailand's recent decisions to make hefty cuts in national and state enterprise budgets in order to curb its current account deficit which, at 8.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1996, was the highest in the region.

Neville said, however, that the market should monitor any future flight from baht-denominated assets to those in dollars that could accompany any future decision by money traders to sell short on the Thai currency.

The analyst said, however, that unlike the Mexican peso, the baht was not historically overvalued against the dollar and Thailand's $39 billion in foreign reserves would serve as a strong cushion against any crisis of confidence in the country.
"The Bank of Thailand will fight very hard to defend the baht and I believe it will succeed in doing so," he said.
